# Sabbāsava Sutta (MN 2 (PTS MN i 6))

**ID:** MN 2 (PTS MN i 6)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Sabbāsava Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** All the Defilements
**PTS:** MN i 6
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn2
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sabbāsava Sutta* ("All the Defilements", MN 2; PTS MN i 6) is the second discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. In this discourse, the Buddha explains that the destruction of the defilements (*āsavas*, or "outflows") is realized through knowing and seeing (*jānato ahaṁ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṁ khayaṁ vadāmi, no ajānato no apassato*) rather than by ignorance [Galasek 2016]. Rather than prescribing a single remedy for every spiritual difficulty, the Buddha explains that different defilements require different approaches, outlining seven distinct methods for abandoning them: by seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, removing, and developing [SuttaCentral]. For instance, certain defilements are abandoned through the proper use of robes and other requisites, which are utilized upon wise reflection simply to protect against cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things [Nattier 2003]. Modern scholars note that the sutta demonstrates the Buddha's internalization and reinterpretation of ethical concepts, reacting against and providing a counterargument to earlier Jain ascetic notions of physical *āsavas* [Galasek 2016].

Curated parallels and cross-language alignments connect MN 2 with several early canonical texts, including Chinese parallels in *Madhyamāgama* 10 (MĀ 10), *Ekottarāgama* 40.6 (EĀ 40.6), and an individual translation, T 31 (*Yiqie liu sheshou yin jing*, "Scripture of the Restraint of All Outflows"), as well as Tibetan parallels in the *Upāyikā* (Up 2.069) [SuttaCentral; Tsukamoto 1979]. DharmaNexus and SuttaCentral both document extensive text reuse across the Pali Canon, most prominently with AN 6.58 (sharing lengthy pericope sequences), AN 4.114, AN 4.157, AN 5.140, and sections of the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22) and *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages of MN 2 with Śamathadeva's *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094), the *Śālistambasūtra*, and the *Śrāvakabhūmi* chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi* in Sanskrit and Tibetan [DharmaNexus]. In later canonical literature, the sutta is cited in the *Sāriputtasuttaniddesa* (Mnd 16) and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 2.2, Kv 2.3) [SuttaCentral].
